Kelsie Hunnicutt discusses a new study in hybrid sticklebacks showing that hybrid incompatibilities drive rapid removal of introgressed alleles following the 2011 Tohoku tsunami in Japan

posts.author_name: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
posts.text: As the climate warms, compound drought and heat wave events are becoming more frequent and intense across the contiguous United States. Areas at high risk for such events are disproportionately poor, unhealthy, and rural. In PNAS: https://ow.ly/nqfA50ZSNx3

Rising sea levels could create new habitat for invasive marine species, says study in @natecoevo.nature.com. The findings suggest that more than two-thirds of newly flooded coastlines could become suitable for non-native species by the end of the century: spklr.io/63326Epu7p 
#Ecology 🌏 🧪
posts.external_title: Global sea-level rise will create a new biological invasion front - Nature Ecology & Evolution
posts.external_description: Sea-level rise may create a new front for the landward expansion of marine invaders into inundated areas. The authors explore the probability of this, projecting that more than two-thirds of inundated land areas would be suitable for 122 non-native animals already established in adjacent marine ecoregions under future sea-level-rise scenarios.
